title: Is there an AI bubble?
question: Does the payback from AI arrive before the balance sheets that financed it run out of time, and if not, where does the shortfall break first?
registration_reason: Review of Nov 23, 2026: the meter's bands are registered (written Nov 17, 2026 with the figure at about 62%), the meter says the growth's basis and reads a month ago on today's companies, and the method's steps carry the page's words
summary: The economy-level case for AI is that demand that already existed, for software above all, is now served faster and cheaper, so the cost pools AI displaces belong in what we call AI demand. A bubble bursts only if that payback comes later or smaller than priced and financed, something forces the market to see it before it closes, and the recognition spreads into equity crashes or insolvencies. This thesis tracks all three, layer by layer, against the reasons it holds.

method.bubble: Companies are borrowing and spending heavily on AI now, betting it will pay back later. It is a bubble if the payback comes later, or smaller, than the lenders can wait for.
method.burst: Share prices fall sharply, or important companies in the chain cannot pay their debts.

steps.title: Demand
steps.question: What is the real upstream demand for AI?
steps.how: We follow the money from the chip makers to the people, companies and governments who finally pay for AI, and project it forward.

steps.title: Costs
steps.question: How much does it cost to meet this demand today, and how much is spent to meet future demand?
steps.how: We add up what the data centres cost each year: the spending on them, spread over the years the equipment lasts, plus a return for the money tied up in them. We also track what could make building them slower or dearer: chips, power, materials and rules.

steps.title: Return on investment timing
steps.question: Combining what we learned in the first two steps: when will demand justify the costs?
steps.how: We set what AI earns (step 1) against what it costs (step 2), year by year, and find the year earnings catch up. We look at two cases: spending keeps growing as fast as it does now, or it stops growing and only replaces worn-out equipment.

steps.title: Can the debt wait?
steps.question: Who holds the debt behind the build-out, and does each company's cash last until AI pays back?
steps.how: We look at who holds the debt that paid for the build-out, and whether each company's cash and borrowing last until AI pays back.

steps.title: Do markets price all of that in?
steps.question: Debt and return-on-investment risks make a bubble only if share prices do not price them in. Do they?
steps.how: We check what share prices already assume, how concentrated and how leveraged the market is, and what in the wider economy could set off or deepen a fall.

rules: Each date uses only what was public by the end of that day. Where a company does not say how much of its spending or revenue is for AI, we use an estimate and say so, with the day we made it.
Every pass mark was written before we looked at the data. When we later changed how a figure is read, the change is listed below with its date and reason.
Projections are marked as projections and always state what they assume.
No AI model computes any number in this report.

changes.reason: G12, written as "not by 2032 counts as 2033", read beyond 2032 on both dates as 0 years (not met), a reading the data cannot give: both years are cut off. Beyond the horizon on both dates now reads unknown. Its first reading also coded a gap already covered as the year read, so two covered readings a year apart read as a year of receding: covered is now its own state. And with the placeholder AI shares written on Nov 11, 2026 applied to every past date (and AI capex counted from 2023), the readings of 2024 and early 2025 were covered by construction: G12 is not read across a date before the shares were written.
G11 read a gap already covered while the cash lasts as 0 years (approaching), against its own rule that such a gap is a payback before the money runs out: it now reads not met.

AI value created added the knowledge-work panel's gross savings (heads times pay) to AI vendors' profit, counting what the panel pays for AI twice; it now adds only savings net of it (the cost ratio's), says the suppliers' and the compute stage's profit apart, and is a ceiling while the labs' losses are not in. AI debt over it was read mostly against the suppliers' margin (90% of value created), which the capex the debt finances pays: it now reads against the value created downstream of the capex (the compute stage's AI profit and the panel's net savings), the suppliers' profit said beside it, and is a floor while the labs' losses are not in. Thresholds are unchanged; no condition reads these two figures.

The savings panel moved to its version 2: each company year's cost lines are checked against its operating margin, a quarter that breaks from the one before and a sale of a business named by hand are flagged, impossible rows are set aside, revenue per unit of labour cost is shown beside the range instead of in it, and savings are scaled to each bucket's own industry. H9's threshold is unchanged.

Aligned after review to one definition, debt against what is spent on AI and what is saved: AI value a year is now what users spend on AI plus what the knowledge-work panel's industries save, the compute stage's AI revenue (the spending that pays for the capex) plus the panel's savings scaled to its industries, net of what it pays for AI, counted in the centre and the low end only once they show beyond the year-to-year noise. It replaces the earlier reading, AI vendors' AI profit plus those savings: demand that already existed served faster and cheaper is AI demand, so the economy's earnings are spending and savings, not vendors' margins. The suppliers' AI profit, paid out of the capex the debt finances, and the compute stage's AI operating profit are said beside it, never in it; applications' AI revenue and the labs' margins beyond the compute they buy are not added. AI debt over it is the economy's debt over earnings, in years, its range from both sides. Thresholds are unchanged; no condition reads these two figures.

After review: the compute stage summed companies that sell to each other, so capacity a builder sells a cloud that resells it was counted twice. What a compute company sells another one whose revenue is counted is now netted out of the seller's AI revenue by the share of its revenue a link states, as known on the day (CoreWeave's sales to Microsoft); a sale with no share stated is left in and said, so the figures may still count some resold capacity twice and AI value a year is no longer called a floor of spending while one is. The compute stage, AI revenue now, the revenue ramp's earned side, the projections and AI value a year change with it. Thresholds are unchanged.

T2 read raises at a lower valuation only as dated events, which nothing writes, so it was always unknown. It now also reads each lab's raises from its own reports: each sale of its shares or notes the words say was made (who bought, when, for how much and at what price a share), known from the report's acceptance and dated only by words about the sale itself or the reader's date for it, never by a period's end or an agreement's date (a raise with no such date is listed, never compared). Shares issued when notes convert, promises to buy, warrants and options exercised, and shares holders resold (secondary sales, tender offers) are not raises. A raise in the window counts when it is priced below an earlier raise of the same stock (both kinds known; a series is a preferred's) stated in the same report, since two reports either side of a stock split state prices on two bases. One report may mix bases too, so a sale stated before a split and a note purchase are never priced, and a price worked out as the amount over the shares is used only when the sale's words state one amount and one count of shares sold, with no holding, most or conversion beside them, in a report that states no split. Below means below by more than either price may be off: half the last stated digit of a stated price, and a 2% margin on one worked out, the rounding of an amount stated to two figures and a count to three. A raise two reports state, or one report states twice, counts and is listed once. A count of zero is a floor over the labs whose raises are read, said with the labs it does not cover, and still unknown when no lab's raises are read: failed or delayed raises and renegotiated contracts are read only as events. T2's data is now partial, not missing. The threshold is unchanged.

xAI became a wholly owned subsidiary of SpaceX on Feb 2, 2026 (a press report of that day, then SpaceX's prospectus of Jun 12, 2026), so the labs layer's member xAI is read through SpaceX from that day, once a source saying so is public, and shown as "xAI (part of SpaceX)"; before it, as itself. Those sources are shown with H3 and T2. T2 counts SpaceX's raises and events only from that day, and a renegotiated contract only when it is for compute (SpaceX's other businesses have contracts of their own), and says xAI's own raises and events before are not read; SpaceX's backers are shown only as known from that day. Its revenue stays its own line, and what SpaceX reports it owes is SpaceX's for all its businesses, so H3 reads no dues for it; where xAI's own figures are is said as of each date (SpaceX had published no report before May 20, 2026). Members and thresholds are unchanged.

X3 counted any financing tie from a supplier to its customer as money the supplier put into it, including financing capacity nothing was drawn of yet (notes that may be issued under a note purchase agreement, none issued) and a facility's size whose drawn part is not stated. Undrawn financing capacity is no money put in: a financing tie now counts only where an amount is drawn or owed; stakes count as before, and assets a company pledged are no tie. The threshold is unchanged.

A layer's strain divided by all the weight known, so a relief or hold condition read as not met (a support found absent) added weight that eased nothing and made the layer read calmer: when H3 first read "not holding" (Anthropic's dues within twelve months against its revenue, Nov 2026), the builders' strain fell from 0.25 (strained) to 0.23 (steady). Learning that a support is missing must never read calmer. A relief or hold condition not met is now left out of the weight the strain is a share of; it still counts as known in the coverage, and it is named as not holding. Bands, thresholds and weights are unchanged.

A layer with under half of its condition weight known now reads "Not enough known" with its share known ("Not enough known, 39% known", never rounded up to 50%) instead of a status. Before, a layer read unknown only under a fifth known, and between a fifth and half its status was shown qualified ("Strained so far, mostly unknown"), so a word rested on a minority of its conditions. Its strain is still computed and shown beside its coverage, never as a status, and it is never counted as strained or steady in the strain-by-layer figure; the figure's value is the most strained layer with half or more known (a layer of companies before the index), and unknown while none has. On Nov 11, 2026 the builders (39% known) read strained so far and the suppliers (33%) steady so far; both now read not enough known. Bands, thresholds and weights are unchanged.

A fiscal year of AI-described federal contracts is read as soon as it has ended, from a fetch made after its end, no longer only from a fetch made 90 days after it. Defense contracts are published about 90 days late, so until then the year's figure is a lower bound and its reading says it can still grow until that day (fiscal 2026, to Sep 30, 2026, can still grow until Dec 29, 2026); from a fetch made then it reads as complete; while it can still grow, its growth on the year before is a lower bound too. On Nov 13, 2026 the government buyer reads fiscal 2026 (about $500M, up at least about 21% on fiscal 2025) instead of fiscal 2025 (about $415M). No condition reads it; thresholds are unchanged.

A builder's runway reads its cash and its cash flows from the same latest report, the latest quarter whose cash and four quarters of operating cash flow and capex to it are both known by the day (ending on the same day), and each row says which quarter and when it was reported. Before, it read the latest cash beside the latest four quarters of cash flows, which could be of different quarters: cash is read from the filings' structured data, the cash flows mostly from quarterly statements, so one could run ahead of the other. Depreciation, no cash but the yardstick of the capex cut to maintenance and of what the business earned, may end a quarter earlier when the latest quarter's is not read, and the row says so. A company whose filings tag its cash only once a year has it read from the same quarterly statements as its cash flows, when a line source names it (Nebius). A later cash whose cash flows are not all read, or later cash flows whose cash is not, is named and left out. A quarter with both more than a quarter before the latest quarter of cash or cash flows it reports is not read from either, as what was raised, borrowed or spent since is not read. Only when no quarter recent enough has both is the latest cash read beside the latest cash flows, saying why, and a cash more than a quarter older than its cash flows still claims no date. On Nov 13, 2026 IREN is read from 2026Q3 ($3.5B of cash at Sep 30, 2026, and the four quarters of cash flows to it, its depreciation to 2026Q2 as its 2026Q3 one is a zero its filing does not support) instead of that cash beside cash flows to 2026Q2, so its at-pace date comes sooner (Apr 2027); Nebius is read from 2026Q2 ($8.0B of cash at Jun 30, 2026, from its quarterly balance sheets) instead of claiming no date. Thresholds are unchanged.

Nebius's interest expense is read from its quarterly income statements, for this one line only. Its filings give structured figures only with its annual report, so they held no quarter of its interest, and H4 and T3 counted its operating losses with its interest unknown. Each quarter is known from its filing's acceptance, and a value revised later only from when the revision was fetched; its sources say where it was read from. On Nov 13, 2026 Nebius's operating income over the four quarters to 2026Q2 (-$669M) covers its interest ($212M) -3.16x, and the builders' combined cover is at most 2.96x instead of 3.05x: the bound no longer straddles H4's 3.0 bar, so H4 reads not holding instead of unknown (as on Oct 31, 2026, just under 3.0x). T3's thinnest cover is still IREN's. Thresholds are unchanged.

AI shares are read as known on each date (the AI attribution's version 2), no longer one placeholder applied unchanged to every date. Each share is a line the company reports times the AI share of that line, quarter by quarter: Nvidia's and AMD's data-centre revenue, Broadcom's chip revenue, Micron's cloud and data-centre memory, the clouds' cloud revenue, each four quarters read as they were public on the day; a window ends at the latest quarter every line of the company reports, the lag said (on Nov 13, 2026 Microsoft reads to 2026Q2: its server and cloud revenue is no longer reported after it; replaced at 11:00 the same day, when Microsoft was read on its Azure revenue from 2026Q3), never whole revenue for a line that is late. The AI share of a line is a filed figure from the day its filing was public (13 entries, each arithmetic on figures quoted from a stored filing: Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue, Microsoft's revenue from OpenAI as a floor, revenue sharing included, Oracle's cloud infrastructure, Amazon's cloud share of additions to property and equipment as a ceiling), else a rule of thumb said with the day it was written; a ceiling or floor narrows it and is never read as the value. Every share is an input of the readings that use it. On Nov 13, 2026 Nvidia reads 84% of its revenue (88% before), AMD 29% (38%), Broadcom 47% (42%) and Microsoft's AI revenue's low end rises with the OpenAI floor. Thresholds are unchanged.

Capex keeps its rule of thumb (no rule reads capex above a pre-AI level yet), each four quarters of capex at its own quarters' shares. The five largest spenders keep the shares written on Nov 11, 2026, flagged as rules of thumb; Amazon's is capped in each calendar year by its cloud's share of additions to property and equipment in that year's annual report (45.6% in 2022, 51.4% in 2023, 62.1% in 2024, 67.8% in 2025), an approximate upper bound as assets are allocated by usage, applied only to that year's quarters and only from the day the report was public. The caps bind in 2022 to 2024, lowering the middle of those years' share (2024 from 50% to 49%); 2025 and 2026 are unchanged. Thresholds are unchanged.

A company's debt is read at the AI share of the four quarters of capex ending at the debt's own quarter, as before in effect, now with those quarters' own shares; a supplier's at its revenue's share over the four quarters ending there (or at the latest quarter its lines report, said). Thresholds are unchanged.

Micron's AI share is read on its cloud memory and core data-centre memory units together, both reported from the reorganisation of its fiscal 2025 (first in 2024Q4), at 60% to 90% AI (the demand chain's range of Nov 12, 2026, a rule of thumb, not a filing); before those units were reported, its whole revenue at the earlier rule of thumb, never both in one window, and growth across the break is unknown. On Nov 13, 2026 that is 45% of its revenue (36% to 55%), its debt following it. Thresholds are unchanged.

Oracle's AI revenue is read on its cloud infrastructure revenue, 50% to 95% of it AI (a rule of thumb written Nov 13, 2026). Its cloud infrastructure revenue is, for each fiscal year, the share of its cloud revenue its annual report states (53% in fiscal 2026, 42% in fiscal 2025, 35% in fiscal 2024, public Jun 22, 2026), and for a quarter whose release states the amount, that amount ($7.4 billion in its first quarter of fiscal 2027; $3.35 billion a year before, from the stated growth of 121%), the other quarters of that fiscal year sharing what its stated fraction leaves, so the year still totals it. Before Jun 22, 2026, and for quarters before fiscal 2024, Oracle reads its whole revenue at the rule of thumb of Nov 11, 2026 (8% to 25%), flagged. On Nov 13, 2026 its AI share of revenue reads 22% (15% to 29%) instead of 15% (8% to 25%): about $5 billion more AI revenue at the centre. Thresholds are unchanged.

Broadcom's debt is read by its purpose, not by what repays it: its term loans and notes financed the VMware acquisition, not AI, so 0% to 10% of it is AI (0% at the centre; a rule of thumb written Nov 13, 2026). Before, it followed its AI revenue share (42%). AI-linked debt falls by about $27 billion at the centre. Its revenue and the chain are unchanged. Thresholds are unchanged.

G12 stays strict: it is not read across a date on which a company counted in the revenue ramp reads a rule of thumb written after that date, and its reason names those companies. Its threshold is unchanged.

A company's filed quarterly results release counts as a filing: an amount it states is reported, and a share computed from stated figures is computed (Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue of $16.7 billion in its third quarter of fiscal 2026 is 80% of its chip revenue, computed). Earnings calls do not count. No condition or headline figure reads the chips stage it moves.

A rule of thumb is dated by the day it was written, never by the filings it leans on, so a date before it reads it said "written after this date"; and before any dated share, a company reads its rule of thumb, said as such. Readings are unchanged; their words say it.
Every quarter of a company's lines is read as reported, with no screen setting aside a quarter out of line with its neighbours. Readings are unchanged.
CoreWeave keeps its rule of thumb of 90% to 100% AI for its revenue, capex and debt; its one reported segment is not read as all of it AI. Readings are unchanged.

AI revenue's growth compares each year under the same rules. For growth only, each company's latest four quarters and the four before are read with only the filed floors and caps that apply in both; one that applies in only one of the two years is set aside in both, and the growth's reason names it. Filed figures that set a share (Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue, Oracle's cloud infrastructure) are data and stay in both years, and the level keeps every bound. Microsoft's revenue from OpenAI in fiscal 2026, a floor in its latest year only, is set aside for its growth until its line changes to Azure (Oct 28, 2026), from when its growth is not compared: on Sep 30, 2026 AI revenue reads $105.5 billion a year, up 47% instead of 50%, the level unchanged; on Aug 31, 2026, on the middle projection with capex cut to maintenance the AI revenue gap closes around 2030 instead of 2029, so the payback comes at least 3 years after a builder's cash could run out instead of 2 (G11). From the same hour Microsoft's AI revenue is read from 2026Q3 on its Azure revenue, the line that follows its server and cloud revenue, which its quarterly report of Oct 28, 2026 no longer states (until then it read to 2026Q2, the change of 07:00 the same day). Its AI share of Azure is a rule of thumb written Nov 13, 2026, set so the same quarter gives the same AI dollars on either line. It is a declared break: AI revenue's growth is never compared across it, so Microsoft is left out of that growth until both years compared are wholly Azure (from the four quarters to 2028Q2); its level counts in full. Thresholds are unchanged.

An agreement to buy a company buys a business, so it is left out of the commitments and listed apart with what else a company's notes state but the sum leaves out. Before, the commitments tier summed every commitment the notes state, so Alphabet's agreements to buy Wiz ($32.0 billion) and Intersect ($4.8 billion) and Eaton's to buy Boyd Thermal ($9.5 billion) counted as commitments: $46.3 billion before AI shares. On Nov 12, 2026 the AI-linked commitments and leases not begun read $1.13 trillion instead of $1.15 trillion; the AI-linked debt and leases, its second total and every figure built on the debt are unchanged. Short-term purchase obligations stay counted, as stated in each company's latest annual report (part due within a year may have been paid since), and the figure now says so. Thresholds are unchanged; no condition reads the commitments.

AI debt over the cash flow its debtors capture is read layer by layer, each layer's AI-linked debt and leases over its own debtors' AI operating cash flow (the same definitions as before), and the figure is the layer with the most years, with its own range. Pooled across the layers it understated the layers that borrowed: the suppliers earn most of the AI cash flow and owe little of the debt, and one layer's cash does not pay another layer's debt. A layer with no AI cash flow is said so, never divided, and the pooled reading is said beside the figure. On Nov 12, 2026 it reads 11.4 years of AI cash flow for the hyperscalers (range 6.3 to 22.6) instead of 2.7 years pooled (range 1.8 to 4.0); the builders read 7.9 years and the suppliers 0.3. Thresholds are unchanged; no condition reads this figure.

T2 now reads dated events from the news held for the labs, beside the raises in their own reports. It counts a raise at a lower valuation, failed, or with a reported delay as before, and three kinds more: a raise closed below the target first reported (its size more than 20% under it, or its valuation more than 10% under it, beyond the rounding of the figures; a ceiling such as "as much as" is no target), counting half; a counterparty ending a binding guarantee, funding commitment or committed purchase made to or for a lab, or cutting its firm amount by half or more, counting one, and cutting it by less, pausing it, or ending a letter of intent or other non-binding plan, counting half; and a renegotiated contract, now only one for compute that a lab ended, cut or deferred, or moved to lower or later payments (an expansion, or a start delayed by a late supplier, is none). One event told by many publications counts once, at the strongest kind of the same raise, commitment or contract in the window, dated by its first public report; the own reporting of a publication on a list written before any story was read counts as a party's confirmation does; a denial on the record by the party said to have acted sets it to zero until that party or a filing confirms it. A model proposes each event and a person reads it before it counts. The page shows each event in WhiteSail's own words with the publisher's link, never the story's text. The count stays a floor, so T2 reads met or not decided yet; the threshold is unchanged.

T2 read no event of xAI before it became part of SpaceX on Feb 2, 2026. Its twelve-month window reaches before that day until Feb 2027, and leaving a lab's own events out would read calmer than what was known: news events about xAI dated before that day are now read as xAI's own, and from that day through SpaceX as before. A raise ended because xAI was being acquired is not a failed raise. The threshold is unchanged.

T6 counts, for the 17 companies of the builders, hyperscalers and suppliers, current reports that past figures can't be relied on (item 4.02) and restatements, one each, and changes of auditor (item 4.01) by what they state: one when the auditor resigned or declined to stand, or a disagreement or reportable event is reported; half when the auditor was dismissed before finishing an audit under way; none, listed, for a planned change. One change of auditor counts once, however many filings report it. Bankruptcy (1.03) and accelerated debt (2.04) are credit events, not doubts about the figures, and are not counted here (T3 reads the builders'). The two foreign issuers' interim and annual reports are searched for the same words, and every match is read by a person before it counts. The count is decided only when every company's whole window was read; while some are, it is a floor, naming what is unread; while none is, it is unknown. Late periodic reports are shown beside it, not scored. The threshold is unchanged.

G7, X2 and H8 read a weekly public dataset of advertised cloud GPU rents (CC BY 4.0): the on-demand rent, the median across providers (each provider once), read only in weeks with five providers or more, never the partial latest week. Generations are Nvidia's data-centre families in release order (Volta, Ampere, Hopper, Blackwell, Rubin), each read on one reference part (A100 80GB SXM, H100 SXM, B200), so a change of mix never moves the price. The newest generation is the latest family listed by five providers or more in the latest full week and in the week a year before; previous and two back are the families before it. Six months are 26 weeks and twelve are 52. Credit is given through the dataset's page, labelled with the attribution it requests, and its licence; no provider is named in WhiteSail's words. Thresholds are unchanged.

Whether the GPU rent dataset's early weeks are approximate is read from its own documentation alone, and as read on Nov 13, 2026, before any of its prices, it marks no week as approximate or entered by hand, so no week is barred from being an end of a change and no reading waits for WhiteSail's own reads to hold its older end: every complete week in the file is read, known from the read that held it. What the documentation says of its history, quoted: each weekly row is "the median of that week's daily values", with "No smoothing, no interpolation"; the history is "weekly snapshots since July 2024 and daily snapshots since July 2026" ("Daily snapshots start on 30 July 2026"); and it says, with no date, that "A small number of providers whose prices rarely change are maintained by hand". Thresholds are unchanged.

Corrected Nov 14, 2026: the dataset lists one entry per GPU model, with no memory size or form factor, so each generation is read on its plain entry (A100, H100, B200), not on the variants named in the change above that chose the dataset (A100 80GB SXM, H100 SXM); its words that a change of mix never moves the price no longer hold. An entry may mix memory sizes and form factors, so a change of mix inside it can move its price; the median across providers is still read as written. A generation's age for X2 still runs from the first general availability of its family's first part (the A100's, May 14, 2020). Thresholds are unchanged.

The GPU rent dataset kept one snapshot a week until Jul 30, 2026 and a snapshot every day from then on, each weekly row the median of its days. A change whose ends fall either side of that day is read as written, not held back, and its words say the change runs across the switch. Thresholds are unchanged.

Each end of a GPU rent change is the median of four weeks in a row, the end week and the three before it, each week the median across providers and listed by five providers or more, so one provider entering or leaving in one week moves an end less. G7 compares the latest four full weeks with the four weeks 26 weeks before; H8 and X2 with the four weeks 52 weeks before, and wait for data until a version of the dataset known by the date holds all four of those older weeks. No change is read over 51 weeks and scaled to a year. Thresholds are unchanged.

X2 compares the rent's fall over twelve months with a six-year straight line's fall over the same year as a share of the value left at the year's start, no longer as a share of the cost: a sixth of its cost is a sixth of the value in the first year and a quarter of the value left at the start of the year it turns three. The generation's age is read at the latest week from the general-availability date of its reference part, as the chip maker announced it, written before any price is read: the A100 on May 14, 2020, and the H100 in Oct 2022 (the maker said on Sep 20, 2022 that availability would begin the next month, so its age is read as a range across Oct 2022). Past six years X2 reads unknown, past the six-year line. Its why says so. The threshold is unchanged.

G4's tracked benchmarks are a public capabilities index (CC BY 4.0) that fits many benchmarks into one score per model. A gain is a model released to the public whose score passes the best of every model released before it by more than the index's stated uncertainty (its interval's low end above that best), or, where none is stated, by more than the last digit shown, said so. Results from testing before a launch count from the public release, as the index's metadata dates it; a gain dated only by an announcement makes the months a ceiling. Each fetch of the index is known from that day, and a refit changes which models were gains only from the fetch that made it. Months since the last gain are days over 30.44. The threshold is unchanged.

H2 and G2 read paid tokens served by the models on one public model marketplace against the price per token in two variations: the price paid per token served, at listed prices (each model's tokens at the median of its hosts' listed prices, over all the tokens), and the price of a fixed level of capability (the lowest such price among models at or above the best capability reached a year before the window began). Volume is read only from a list of every model's tokens. Each variation is read alone; the condition is decided only when both are read and give the same status, and otherwise reads not decided yet with both shown, as an estimate straddling its bar does. Thresholds are unchanged.

G2's why asks for two quarters in a row so that one price cut does not decide it, while its window is two quarters. Read as one change over the two quarters, a single step down in the price of a fixed capability would meet it on two readings running. G2 now reads the highest of the change over the window and the two quarter-on-quarter changes of usage times price: met only when it shrank or held in each quarter, approaching when it grew 25% or less over the two quarters and in each, so the bar keeps its meaning on the window and G2 can never be approaching while H2 holds. H2 keeps the change over the whole window. Thresholds are unchanged.

X6 reads margin loans and other receivables at securities brokers and dealers from the US central bank's quarterly financial accounts, with every vintage, in place of the brokers' regulator's monthly margin table, which is not read. A measure defined differently from those tables (it adds other receivables), at about half their level, and quarterly: only its own rise over four quarters is read, against the same bar, and a missing year-earlier quarter reads unknown. The threshold is unchanged.

Nebius's and TSMC's debt is read from their latest quarterly balance rows. TSMC reports in New Taiwan dollars: balances are converted at the rate on the quarter's last day and flows at the quarter's average, the central bank's noon buying rates in New York, each known from the later of the row and the rate; a row in another currency than the company reports in is set aside, and no sum adds amounts in two currencies. A zero no filing backs is set aside, and no quarter is set aside for being out of line with its neighbours; a total whose make-up changes between quarters is replaced by its parts; the year-end quarter is checked against the annual report, whose figure is read where they differ, and leases found inside the debt fields are taken out. Thresholds are unchanged.

T3's credit events are read from the builders' current reports by their item numbers alone. A company whose balance sheets are read, that tags no debt line in any report read, and whose annual report's notes, read in full for debt, state no debt maturity and no loan it owes, owes no borrowings: its debt reads $0, computed, said beside it (Arista). A financing an annual report's notes state is added beside the debt only when no balance sheet read can already hold it: when the report puts it outside the debt, when it is a deposit or prepayment the company must repay, or when the debt read is as of the report's own year-end or earlier and the financing was entered after that year-end or is neither a lease nor a loan. One read beside a later balance sheet may already be in its debt or lease lines, and a lease or loan entered by the year-end is already in that year-end's lease or debt lines, so each is listed, not added (CoreWeave's $1.5B vendor financing, Applied Digital's $58.5M Texas Capital loan, IREN's $102M and $96M vendor financings, Micron's $1.6B vehicle financing, and on 2025 days Amazon's $151M financing).

An annual report's notes stated in another currency than the US dollar (TSMC's, in New Taiwan dollars) are converted at the rate on its fiscal year's last day, known from the later of the report and the rate, as quarterly balances are since the change of Nov 14, 2026 that reads Nebius's and TSMC's debt from their quarterly rows; before, they were left out and said. Each figure is in its own currency: one whose words name US dollars alone (TSMC's capital spending plan) is not converted. Their lease present values never stand in where the debt rows may include leases. TSMC's temporary receipts from customers, a prepayment on its balance sheet its notes do not put inside its debt, count beside its debt as Micron's customer deposits do: about $6.1B at its 2025 year-end, $1.8B of it AI-linked.
A builder whose debt is read from a source's quarterly rows (Nebius) has what it borrowed since its maturities schedule read from the same rows.

A runway spreads an annual report's maturities from the fiscal year-end that report covers: the day its document's name states, else its latest quarter whose results were public by the day after it was filed. Applied Digital's fiscal 2025 ends May 31, 2025, not Feb 28; Alphabet's fiscal 2024 ends Dec 31, 2024.

Circular financing shows a lender from outside the AI companies when a member's notes name it and it is a company among the companies read; a financing the notes put inside the debt is owed in full though the reading gave nothing drawn; an amount in another currency than the US dollar is not shown as dollars.

X1's leading reading, how much of the builders' backlog rests on one customer, is read from their annual reports' notes (a customer's stated share of the remaining performance obligations, weighted by each builder's backlog), never from a share of revenue. It is not scored.

X1 reads each builder's backlog due within twelve months at its annual report's own year-end, at the share that report states for it, against the revenue of the four quarters after. The latest report's share had been applied to the backlog a year before the latest quarter, a backlog it was not stated for (IREN's 17.65% against a backlog 26 times smaller).

A customer's share of revenue a filing states is known from the filing's acceptance, and the sale it describes counts from then, not from when WhiteSail first held the link: CoreWeave's 67% from Microsoft (its 2025 annual report, accepted Mar 2, 2026) is netted from that day, not from Nov 1, 2026.

A financing's entry date is read only from entry words in its quote, never from a maturity, an amendment or a deposit (Nov 14, 2026), and never as a day after the report that states it was public: a later date in its quote is when the financing ends or a plan, not when it was entered.

G7 shows the change in private data-centre construction spending over twelve months, at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, from the government's construction spending tables: the figures of the latest release read, each known from that release's day (or the day the table was last changed, if later), never dated back, so no earlier date reads them. It is shown beside G7 and never scored.

The 10-year Treasury yield, as read here, is published on the next business day, so each day's figure is known from 23:00 UTC of the next weekday not observed as a US federal holiday, never from its own day. T4 reads it so on every date; its threshold is unchanged. The corporate bond spreads shown beside T3, T4 and X4 are dated the same way.

T3 shows the change in the high-yield and BBB corporate bond spreads over six months, T4 the investment-grade spread's, and X4 the change in the spread of the riskiest bonds (CCC and lower) over six months, the net share of banks tightening standards for business loans, and the change in banks' commercial and industrial loans over twelve months, each revision known from its release. Each is shown beside its condition and never scored.

G8 shows the change over twelve months in the generating capacity operating or on standby and in the electricity sold to commercial customers, and R6 the change in the average price of electricity to commercial customers: the figures of the latest monthly edition of the government's electricity statistics read, each known from that edition's release day as its page states it, never dated back. Each is shown beside its condition and never scored.

T1 reads each hyperscaler's capex outlook from its last eight earnings releases, each known from its release's acceptance: a cut is a later outlook for the same year whose midpoint is more than 2% below the one before, made within the last two quarters. Only a release's outlook lines are read, and each amount must be stated in its quote. Microsoft states no capex outlook in its releases (it gives one on the call, not read), so while it is unread the count is a floor: met or not decided yet, never not met.

G8 reads the builders' total active power delivered against what they guided, from their last eight earnings releases (contracted, secured or leased power and single sites never counted). A small model reads the releases, so a figure counts only once a person has accepted it, and from that moment; until then G8 is not read and says how many figures wait. Nebius files its results on a form the release reader does not read.

R1-R4 and T7 read public actions from the news held for the AI layers' companies, chipmaking tools and the main markets' utilities (a year read, at most 150 stories a run): copyright judgments, settlements and injunctions; export rules; antitrust inquiries, suits and blocked deals on the AI deals; large-load tariffs and moratoria in the main data-centre markets; urgent rules or investigations after an AI incident (an investigation counting half). A small model proposes each and a person confirms it; an action counts from its confirmation. The news held is a market feed, not a register of rulings or decisions, so each reading is a floor: met, or not decided yet, never not met.

X4 shows beside it the median share of the listed private-credit funds' investments on non-accrual status, at fair value, from each fund's latest report within two quarters, known from the report's acceptance. Never scored.

What a lab with no own report read (OpenAI) has committed to buy is read from the news held: a contract's seller and total, from the sentence that reports it, kept as an estimated commitment once a person names its seller. A total over a term is never spread over the years: a deal with no amount stated for a year is named among the lab's commitments with no schedule, not counted in what it must pay within a year. Anthropic's own report and xAI's holder are read instead of the news.

The stress test's capex cut is traced to the suppliers whose buyers' shares of their revenue are quoted (Nvidia and Arista): each loses, a year, its revenue of the last four quarters times each buyer's share times the part of that buyer's capex the cut takes away, with the shares' ranges. An analyst's estimate of a share ranges from half of it to one and a half times it; a filing's shares for unnamed customers range between the shares it states. The other suppliers are named and not traced. No condition reads it.

The demand chain's applications stage reads a floor of its AI revenue: what the software companies' own earnings releases say they earn from AI (a revenue, an annual recurring revenue, a run rate, an annual contract value, or a share of revenue), each from the sentence that states it, the latest within six months. A run rate, a recurring revenue or a contract value counts as a year; a quarter's revenue counts four times. A figure influenced by AI, a pipeline, a backlog, an outlook or a figure nearly reached is never counted. The end buyers, whose AI spending no source states, read at least the larger of the models' and the applications' floors, never their sum. No condition reads either.

A company's quarter whose source dates it on the quarter's last day, before any report was public, is known from the day the company announced that quarter's results (the first day of its earnings calendar with an actual revenue, within 100 days of the quarter's end), as the end of that day; with no such day it stays set aside. SK hynix's quarters and the foreign filers of the knowledge-work panel (Infosys, Wipro, Globant, IBEX) are read from then. A company whose ticker's own record was merged into another listing is read under the record that holds its ticker (News Corporation).

G13 added at the owner's request: how long each year's AI investment takes to earn back, and whether that time grows. Its threshold (20% a year or more met, 5% to 20% approaching) was written before any Time-to-ROI was computed. Its first reading rule added up all the money from 2023, the earliest earned back first; tried on made-up figures in which revenue and investment grow at the same pace, it grew in the first years all the same (the count starts in 2023), so before registration it was replaced by each year's own investment against the revenue earned after it, which stays constant when both grow alike. On the data both rules read met (+64% and +24% a year). 2022 is not a year of it: the report counts AI capex from 2023, and 2022's capex at today's AI shares would make the trend look better than it is.

The five largest spenders' AI share of capex (Amazon, Oracle, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft) is at least the part of each quarter's capex above a pre-AI level, their 2022 capex grown 10% a year, computed from their own filed capex as known on the day. The rule of thumb stays the middle where it sits above that floor, else the floor is the middle. The rule was chosen after seeing what it gives over the four quarters to 2026Q3. Debt that follows capex follows it. On Nov 19, 2026: AI-linked debt $765B instead of $671B, the capital charge on the AI capex $248B instead of $230B, AI-linked debt 6.9 years of AI value instead of 6.0, and Time-to-ROI growing 31% a year instead of 24%. Thresholds are unchanged.

Where a builder's filings state its AI revenue, its AI share of revenue is read from them, quarter by quarter, from each filing's acceptance: IREN's AI cloud revenue (88% of its revenue in July to September 2026, against a rule of thumb of 15% to 50%), Nebius's AI cloud business (91% in 2025) and Applied Digital's revenue outside its crypto-mining hosting (75% in its fiscal 2026). Quarters no filing covers keep the rule of thumb. On Nov 19, 2026: IREN's AI share of revenue over the four quarters to 2026Q3 is 45% instead of 30%, Applied Digital's 80% instead of 60%, Nebius's to 2026Q2 87% instead of 85%; AI revenue is $111.3 billion a year instead of $111.0 billion, growing 63% instead of 62%, so the earliest year the gap can close is 2029 instead of 2030 (the middle stays 2033). Thresholds are unchanged.

Wording only, asked by the owner on Nov 19, 2026: the end buyers' software measures say "software companies" for the survey's industry of companies whose main business is making and selling software, whose official name readers did not know. The series read, the figures and every rule are unchanged; the demand chain's words are part of the digest, so the change is a new version.

G14 added at the owner's request: the AI revenue in 2030 that the AI basket's share prices need, set on the report's own projection of AI revenue for that year. Its method and threshold were the owner's four picks of Nov 19, 2026, written before any of it was read: the AI premium is market value above each company's 2022 average grown 7% a year; it is discounted at the 10-year Treasury yield plus 5 points, with AI profits growing in a straight line to 2030 and valued at 20 times earnings from then; 40% (30% to 50%) of AI revenue ends as profit in these companies; needing more than the high projection is met, more than the middle approaching.

AI revenue counts an estimated lift inside existing businesses (Meta's advertising, Alphabet's search and YouTube ads, Microsoft 365), which it did not count before: Meta's AI capex was counted with none of its AI earnings. Each line is set against its own pre-AI trend, its 2022 quarters grown at its compound growth from 2019 to 2022; from 2023, half (25% to 75%) of its revenue above that trend over a window counts as AI, never below zero. Microsoft 365's renamed lines are joined to its Office line by their fiscal 2023 as its 2025 annual report restates it. The rule was written before any of it was read. On Nov 19, 2026: Meta's advertising ran $21.3 billion above its trend over the four quarters to 2026Q2 and Microsoft 365 $8.7 billion over three quarters to 2026Q2, so about $15 billion counts ($7.5 billion to $22.5 billion); Alphabet's search and YouTube ads ran below theirs. AI revenue is about $126.3 billion a year instead of $111.3 billion, up 79% instead of 63%; with capex at its recent pace the gap closes around 2032 instead of not by 2032, around 2029 instead of 2030 with capex cut to maintenance; AI-linked debt is 6.1 years of AI value instead of 6.9; Time-to-ROI's growth reads 22% a year, its range now across the bar (not decided, from met). Thresholds are unchanged.

The report is published step by step. This version holds the opening and the demand step: its twelve conditions and its two figures (AI revenue, and AI value a year). The other steps' conditions, figures and chains wait on the report's parent branch and come back as each step is published. No answer is given until all five are. No threshold, recipe or rule of the demand step changed.

The sources only the later steps read leave this step's branch with them: GPU rents and the chip generations' reference parts, electricity, data-centre construction, power delivered, private-credit non-accruals and the debt's fair values. The chip generations' list was read with the definition, so the change is a new version. No condition, figure, threshold or rule of the demand step changed.

The demand step's first fine-tuning. The chips stage no longer adds the chip designers' own suppliers: TSMC and SK hynix sell mainly to Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom, so they are listed beside the stage, not added (demand-chain version 5). Networking and power, read on three companies, is a floor. OpenAI's revenue is read from its third quarter of 2026 (about $10 billion, a press estimate known from Nov 10, 2026) instead of its 2025, so the labs are read on 2026 figures: H10 reads about 0.67x from Nov 11, 2026 (0.45x before), still not decided, as its low end is under the bar. No threshold or rule changed.

XAI's revenue is read from SpaceX's quarterly reports, which do not state it apart, as a range: its low end the SI segment's AI solutions and infrastructure line in 2026Q1 (before SpaceX sold cloud compute or owned Cursor), its high end the quarter's line less the cloud services to its largest customer and Cursor's revenue. SpaceX's cloud services to that customer count in the compute stage (the AI attribution's spacex-cloud-in-compute). No threshold or rule changed.

Every lab is read on its latest quarter at a yearly rate, the same basis for each, never nine months averaged beside another lab's quarter. Anthropic's quarters are read from its registration statements' quarterly statements of operations (its 2026Q2 from Oct 26, its 2026Q3 from Nov 2), so its rate is about $68B a year where nine months averaged gave $44B; H10 reads about 0.84x. No threshold changed.

End demand is counted once where a final user pays, apart from the supply chain that serves it, never split by company. H10 now reads the share of the compute stage's AI revenue paid by end users: one less the labs' compute bought with money they raised (each lab's operating loss, up to its compute spending; the whole loss where its compute spending is not stated) over that revenue. Its bar, holding at or above 75% and weakening at or above 50%, was the owner's pick, made after a rough preview of about 65% was shown to him. The end buyers stage reads that end demand in place of the floor taken from the labs. It replaces the labs' revenue over the compute stage's (0.5 and 0.3).

Every lab's operating result is read on one measure, the adjusted operating result, before stock-based compensation and other non-cash costs (the closest the labs state to cash), where OpenAI's second quarter included stock-based compensation and its third did not, and Anthropic's filed results included it. Anthropic's adjusted result is a profit ($2.5 billion in its third quarter, from its registration statement), so its investors pay none of its compute; OpenAI's second quarter is read adjusted ($10.1 billion lost) once known. Where only a result with stock-based compensation in it is known, it is read and H10 is a floor. H10 reads about 67% on Nov 19, 2026 (from about 65%), still not decided. (Version 17 is the full report's, on its own branch.) No threshold changed.

The demand chain's six stages are the market map's six columns, with the same names and companies (demand chain version 6): foundries and memory, processors, networking and power, the clouds and AI builders, the AI labs, the clouds reselling the labs' models, and the final buyers. Applications (software) leaves the chain. No condition reads a stage it changes, and no threshold changed.

Asked by the owner on Nov 22, 2026: the market map adds the companies that were missing (demand chain version 7). A first stage, chipmaking tools; Samsung among the memory makers; Marvell, Cisco, Coherent, Lumentum, Credo, GE Vernova, Schneider Electric and Siemens Energy among the processors, networking and power, each at a rule of thumb for its AI share written today. Listed beside their stages and never added, so no dollar is counted twice: the server assemblers, the data-centre landlords and hosts, the private builders and site owners, and Google's Gemini. Amazon resells the labs' models too. The market map's other views come back with the banks the filings name and each company's balance-sheet debt. Numbered 22 so as not to share a number with the full report's versions 20 and 21. No condition reads a stage it changes; end demand and H10 read the compute stage and the labs, unchanged.

Asked by the owner on Nov 22, 2026: a company shown on the market map is a company counted (demand chain version 8). Each intermediary counts for what it adds: the server assemblers at the share of their AI revenue they keep beyond the chips inside, a rule of thumb written today; the data-centre landlords and hosts, suppliers of space and power the clouds pay, whole at their AI share, in the stage now named Chips, servers, power and space. The companies with no figures read leave the market map until they are read. No condition reads the stage; end demand and H10 are unchanged.

Asked by the owner on Nov 22, 2026: the stage of clouds reselling the labs' models leaves the demand chain (version 9). It repeated part of the labs' own revenue and had no figure per cloud; the AI labs stage says it includes the labs' sales through the clouds. Alphabet is shown with the AI labs and not added, since Alphabet does not report its models' revenue apart and it is counted with the clouds. No condition reads the stage; end demand and H10 are unchanged.

Asked by the owner on Nov 22, 2026: end demand adds what AI application startups keep a year after paying for models and compute, an outside estimate (Menlo Ventures' enterprise AI application spending less the labs' own apps, the startups' 61% of the rest, at ICONIQ's 45% to 59% gross margins for AI products), counted from the day it was public (Nov 3, 2026). What the startups pay the labs is already in the labs' revenue, so only the value they add is counted. H10 reads what investors pay of the compute stage, not end demand, and is unchanged.

Asked by the owner on Nov 23, 2026: usage times price is read, so H2 and G2 no longer wait for data. While the marketplace's weekly paid tokens cannot be read (its terms forbid storing them), both read the three labs' tokens times what each token is paid, which is their revenue (Revenue trends: Anthropic's filings, OpenAI's press figures, Google's stated tokens times the price paid), over the same window of two quarters: H2 the window's ratio, G2 the highest of each quarter's ratio and the window's. Read from the labs, the two marketplace variations are not needed to decide them; the marketplace's figures take their place again once read.

Asked by the owner on Nov 23, 2026: the report no longer reads work done with fewer people (its section was removed the same day), so the two reasons it holds that read it leave the demand step: H1 (software and services companies' selling and admin costs falling as a share of revenue) and H9 (office-work companies avoiding hires against a control panel). No other condition, layer weight or threshold changes. AI value created still counts the knowledge-work panel's net savings; no condition reads it.

After the review of Nov 23, 2026: the words the demand step's meter reads AI revenue's growth with (stalling up to 10%, slowing above it to 30%, growing above it to 60%, booming above 60%; a growth at a line takes the lower word) join the definition as the figure's bands. They were written on Nov 17, 2026 for the page alone, when the growth read about 62%, just above the booming line; from this version a change to them is a new version, logged here with its date and reason. The meter also says what share of the figure its growth compares and who is left out, and reads a month ago on today's companies where the companies compared then were not today's. The method's steps are reworded to the page's: the demand step no longer says it checks 39 office-work companies (version 27 removed that check), and the questions of the steps to come are the page's. No reading, threshold or weight changes.

Savings count in the centre and, above zero, in the low end only once they show beyond the year-to-year noise of the years before AI; until then, in the high end only, and never subtracted. Beside it, never in it: the chip, memory, networking and power makers' AI profit, $266.4B a year (range $231.6B to $302.2B), is paid out of the capex the AI-linked debt finances; the compute stage's AI operating profit, $38.8B a year (range $23.5B to $54.5B), is part of the revenue counted here.

Meta's latest annual report says no customer was 10% or more of its revenue, so what it sells any one of them is less than that. second_order.detail: Not read: Kyndryl (no fiscal 2022 heads and revenue); Wipro (its years after the anchor have a gap). Years kept out of the fit and carried at the company's own pace: 36 for a move over 35% (an acquisition, a divestiture or a bad count: Aon fiscal 2017, Aon fiscal 2018, Concentrix fiscal 2023, Concentrix fiscal 2024 and 32 more); 12 for a quarter that breaks from the one before beyond its season (a business sold or restated part-way through a year: Broadridge Financial Solutions fiscal 2018, Broadridge Financial Solutions fiscal 2019, Darden Restaurants fiscal 2020, Darden Restaurants fiscal 2021 and 8 more); 2 moved by a sale of a business not read yet (Fidelity National Information Services fiscal 2024 and 2025, the Worldpay separation (announced in July 2023, closed in January 2024) moved its revenue to continuing operations inside fiscal 2022 and its heads after). Company years left out of the cost ratio: 22 whose cost lines add up to more than their costs (one minus the operating margin) by over 3% of revenue, lines that overlap: Arthur J. Gallagher (10 years), Marsh (4 years), IBEX (2 years), S&P Global (2 years), Interpublic Group of Companies (1 year), New York Times (1 year), Omnicom (1 year) and Verisk Analytics (1 year); 40 whose lines fall 10% of revenue or more short of their costs, missing a cost line: Willis Towers Watson (10 years), Verisk Analytics (8 years), News Corp (6 years), Marsh (5 years), TaskUs (4 years), Aon (3 years), New York Times (2 years), ServiceNow (1 year) and TTEC (1 year). Cost-ratio steps over 10 points of revenue in a year, held at the company's own pace in the cost ratio: Autodesk fiscal 2019 and Autodesk fiscal 2020. Largest contributors to the middle estimates, in heads avoided: heads against revenue on 2017-2022 (14,000 in all): TTEC 16,000, Arthur J. Gallagher -12,000 and Genpact -11,000; the cost ratio on 2017-2022 (23,000 in all): Salesforce 16,000, Moody's 5,500 and Maximus 3,300. Beside the range, never in it: revenue per unit of labour cost on 2016-2019 reads 47,000 heads avoided, of which the control's reading gives 110,000 (the panel's own, -62,000): its control is read with the wage index of other industries and heads tied one to one to revenue, so its difference rests on the control alone. Beside the range, never in it: revenue per unit of labour cost on 2017-2022 reads 160,000 heads avoided, of which the control's reading gives 177,000 (the panel's own, -18,000): its control is read with the wage index of other industries and heads tied one to one to revenue, so its difference rests on the control alone. Acquisitions and restructuring charges are not read yet, so a year moved by them is caught only by the flags. Head counts are annual, from the annual reports. IT services firms, which charge by the head, show 4,700 heads fewer than their revenue needed: work moving off labour-priced suppliers, counted apart and never added to the savings. Savings are scaled only to the panel's own industries in the United States, industry by industry and each estimate with its own sign: each industry's net savings over its own wage bill, times its industry's wage bill. The heads avoided are the median and range across both estimators: head counts (against revenue) and the cost ratio (every operating cost against the years before AI, so net of what the companies pay for AI); AI value a year counts only the cost ratio's, the figure beside them. While the estimate is within the year-to-year noise of the years before AI, the savings' range runs down to zero at least.

token_revenue.rule: One rule for every provider. Tokens grow at the pace of the latest quarter, read from the lab's stated revenue and put at a yearly rate, the pace halving every year toward 10% a year. Revenue per token is what a token is paid, cached input and coding agents' mix counted, and falls as tokens grow, as the price paid for closed-weight models on OpenRouter fell while their tokens grew. Revenue is tokens times price, never drawn forward itself. The range around it moves the two assumptions that move it most, each on its own: the pace halving every nine months or every fifteen months, and the price falling a quarter faster or a quarter slower as tokens grow.
token_revenue.note: Revenue per token is what a token of the workhorse model is paid: its list price with coding agents' cached input and mix counted (after SemiAnalysis); discounts and cheaper models make it lower still. Tokens are revenue over that price, estimated; where a lab states its API's tokens a minute, they are shown beside as a check. Google's tokens a quarter are the average of the rates it stated at the quarter's start and end (for the quarter before and for the quarter), times its minutes, the first quarter with a stated rate at that rate alone; its revenue is those tokens times the price paid, estimated.

room_to_grow.rule: Revenue from a kind of buyer is how many pay times what each pays. This counts how many more could pay, at what each pays now: a ceiling's multiple is the most who could pay over those paying now, and it is reached in the first projected quarter whose revenue is that multiple of the latest quarter's, each buyer's share of revenue held where it is now.
